posts.name: Gaurab Chakrabarti
posts.text:
King Slide, a Taiwanese maker of kitchen drawer slides, owns 70-90% of the market for high-end AI server rails. On Oct 30 it approved more than $600 million for what it plans as the world’s largest rail factory.

If you were building a King Slide competitor, you could buy the steel and the steel balls. You would have to build the molds, the stamping and plating lines and the assembly machines yourself. You would also have to design around its roughly 3,750 patents.

A server rail works like a drawer slide: three steel strips nest on steel balls. The two rails on either side of an AI server are 6.1 mm thick and hold a chassis of more than 40 kg. Each rail has more than 100 parts, and none can be off by more than 0.02 mm. Pulled all the way out, the rail holds the server from one end, and Nvidia’s next racks are heavier while the rails have to get thinner because liquid-cooling pipes take up the space.

Nan Juen, another Taiwanese furniture-slide maker, had made server rails since 2002. When it went after cloud servers in 2012, it found no major customer for six years because the brands had already picked their rail suppliers. It reached Nvidia’s GB200 rack in 2024.

A rail sells for under $100 and protects a rack that costs millions. In the second quarter King Slide’s gross margin was 87.4%. It still sells kitchen drawer slides.

posts.text:
Nate Boerkircher had one scholarship offer coming out of high school and it was from a Division II school, and six years later Jacksonville took him in the second round.

He grew up in Aurora, Nebraska. The 2020 census put the population at 4,678. When the four Boerkircher kids went through the high school there, the graduating classes were around 100.

He had knee surgery before his junior season and missed the start of it. He came back in time to catch two touchdown passes from his quarterback, a kid named Baylor Scheierman who now plays for the Boston Celtics, and Aurora finished 13-0.

Nobody offered. He did not care.

"I was shocked when he said he's going Division I or he wasn't going to play and just go to college," his mother Sherry said.

So he walked on at Nebraska in 2020.

His older brother Ian had walked on there the year before, after starting out at Division II Nebraska-Kearney.

Ian wore 58. Nate wore 49.

On September 3, 2022, Nate caught a 19 yard touchdown pass against North Dakota, and Ian came sprinting off the sideline to grab him.

"Thank God they got that picture," Ian said. "I'm running onto the field to celebrate with him because I had the biggest adrenaline rush of my life seeing him score."

The newspapers in Lincoln and Omaha ran no comments from Nate that night. Nobody asked.

"That was one of the most amazing days," Sherry said, "because my boys were on the field at the same time for Nebraska and they got to celebrate together and play together."

Nebraska put him on scholarship before the 2023 season. Year four.

He caught 11 passes over the next two years. In five seasons there he had 19 catches total.

He put his name in the portal in December of 2024 and called a coach he knew at Texas A&M himself. Three games into that season, on fourth down with 13 seconds left in South Bend, he caught an 11 yard touchdown to beat Notre Dame 41 to 40. His parents had driven from Nebraska and were watching from the opposite corner.

"Very emotional," his father Matt said. "It's still emotional. Right underneath Touchdown Jesus."

He finished his college career with 38 catches.

Jacksonville drafted him 56th overall anyway. The reaction online was not kind, because almost nobody had heard of him and the draft boards had him going on the last day.

"He's been a steady climber all of his life," Matt said.

Before this season, his father and his brother had never been to an NFL regular season game in their lives.

TONIGHT, in Baltimore, Nate Boerkircher caught a 52 yard pass. It was the longest play of the game and it set up the first touchdown.

Somewhere in Nebraska there is a photograph of his brother running onto a field to hug him.

posts.text:
The TGA isn’t the binding constraint (except in an inane legal sense you already know). The private sector resource base is. The govt monetizes that base by taxing it or issuing debt against it. Either way it needs a taxable resource base to run its balance sheet against. Without one you just get inflation. 

Now, you'll reply they don't need to tax it because they can issue money. But debt is just a claim on the same resource base the pvt sector already monetized when they created it. If you never tax it, the price level does the taxing for you when you create more money on the same resources. 

That’s why ‘taxes don’t fund spending’ is misleading at best. The resource base the pvt sector creates is the very thing that allows the govt to operate a large balance sheet in the first place.

posts.name: Cullen Roche
posts.text:
Just remember: 

1. Every economic entity must fund its balance sheet. MMT misconstrues this concept by treating central government spending as self-funding because the sovereign issues the unit of account, but this ignores liability management: money creation injects liabilities into the private sector that alter asset prices, yield curves, and inflation expectations. Spending without credible funding mechanisms is not a free lunch; it is an inflation tax.

2. While loans create deposits endogenously, banks face strict liquidity and capital constraints. A bank must fund deposit outflows at clearing, manage reserves, and hold regulatory capital against risk-weighted assets. Credit expansion is constrained by balance sheet profitability and solvency risk, not an infinite creation tap.

3. Taxes don't just 'drive currency demand'; the real productive tax base defines a nation's fiscal space. A sovereign's ability to run persistent deficits depends entirely on an endogenous, highly productive private sector creating goods, services, and wealth to back that unit of account. Deficit capacity is a derivative of private-sector productivity, which is why the US can sustain deficits that developing economies like Somalia cannot.
 
4. The MMT claim that 'government deficits equal private financial surpluses' is an accounting truism, not an economic virtue. By definition, any borrower's liability is another party’s financial asset. Just as household borrowing creates financial assets for the non-household sector, government borrowing creates non-government assets. The critical question isn't whether the ledger balances, it always does, it's whether the debt fuels real output growth or simply inflates nominal claims against a fixed resource base. 

5. Real economic wealth is constrained by what the private sector produces. Since government *often* absorbs real resources (labor, capital, materials) rather than producing them, public spending redistributes or competes for private-sector output. Therefore, fiscal policy is bound by productive supply, and expanding nominal claims faster than real output inevitably degrades the currency. Private sector output constraints govt balance sheet expansion. See #3.

posts.name: Alok Agrawal
posts.text:
The recent drawdown in AI-capex-tied equities, and the open schadenfreude (as well as posts of remorse) that has accompanied it, got me thinking.

You are never as good as you think you are when you are winning, or as bad as you think you are when you are losing. The roll of the dice plays a far larger role in investment and life outcomes than most people care to admit.

Michael Mauboussin captures this dynamic brilliantly in *The Success Equation*, where he untangles the interplay of skill and luck across markets, sports, and business. His most counterintuitive insight is the “paradox of skill”: as any competitive field matures and the baseline level of talent, data, and analytical rigor rises, the gap between the best and the average participant narrows. Paradoxically, as skill becomes more uniform at the top, luck becomes a bigger determinant of the final outcome.

Nowhere is this clearer than in investing. At the institutional level, hundreds of smart, relentless analysts are parsing the same filings, tracking the same alternative data, and building similar models. When everyone at the table is highly capable, small exogenous variables—a sudden macro regime shift, an unexpected regulatory headline, or the exact timing of a liquidity squeeze—can turn a mediocre thesis into a windfall, or a rigorous, high-probability bet into a painful drawdown.

Looking backward, we hate randomness. We invent clean narratives about superior foresight during bull runs and fatal flaws during drawdowns so the uncertainty feels less threatening. Recognizing the true weight of luck doesn’t mean abandoning rigor—it means judging yourself by the quality of your process rather than the noise of a single outcome. It demands humility when your numbers look brilliant and resilience when the tape goes against you. Skill and effort matter enormously, and so does the roll of the dice. Both are true at once.

And my final advice - while it's a good idea to let your winners run, take profits along the way.  It's more important to live to fight another day.

Excellent set of arguments. We should definitely reduce FPI taxation on cap gains to zero like nearly all other countries do.

I also think bond taxation through mutual funds is actually worth revisiting since bonds have some inherent risk (fixed deposits don't). But the data is clear: Bank FDs are simply the biggest place that people invest in, period.

The data for FY26:
Households invested 15 lakh crore in FDs
They invested 9 lakh crore in EPF/PPF, which is mostly invested in bonds (govt + some corporate)
They invested 3 lakh crore in NSC/Post Office deposits which is just fixed income
About 5 lakh cr went into insurance (which is partly fixed income/partly equity)

They invested net 5 lakh crore into equity+mutual funds
(Source: RBI Bulletin)

Equity is a very small part of household saving incremental allocations (just 12% of the 43 lakh crore additional savings by households in FY26 went into equity)

We can make equity relatively unattractive, but it's still too small a portion of household incremental flows, even compared worldwide. We should promote the bond market by lower taxation perhaps (allowing debt funds a lower capital gains tax) but not promote FDs any more - they are a HUGE part of all incremental allocations.
